conflict_topics: ventilation responsibility / standing rule on extractor use
risk of wetting laundry if window opened / permission to move drying rack
dialogue_quality_notes: Agents give concrete practical reasons (headaches, tutoring schedule, risk of wet laundry, cooking ruining) which grounds requests.
Some useful concessions: A turned on extractor and agreed to 10 minutes post-cooking this time; B softened from 20 to 15 then accepted 10 for this instance.
Positions are consistently stated and roles/facts (who has stove, who has laundry, window state) remain clear.
evaluation.final_reason: Although A agreed to use the extractor and to 10 minutes post-cooking for this instance, there is no agreement on a standing ventilation rule, no consent to move or open the window while C's laundry is drying, and a new urgent stove-access timing conflict (D needs the stove sooner than A can finish). Multiple incompatible demands remain unsettled.
position_change_notes: Agent A softened: turned the extractor on immediately and agreed to 10 minutes post-cooking for this instance, but refused a general 15–20 minute standing rule (Turns 1, 3, 5, 10).
Agent B softened demands: moved from requesting 20 minutes to 15 and then accepted 10 minutes this time while asking for advance notice (Turns 2, 4, 6).
Agent C remained firm about not opening the window or moving the drying rack now due to tutoring (Turns 8, 12).
Agent D maintained need for stove within a tight time window but did not offer a concrete accommodation; the stove-access timing conflict emerged in Round 6 (Turns 9, 14).

round_scores.evidence: Agent A refused a standing rule but turned the extractor on (Turn 1). Agent B requested a 20-minute post-cooking extractor runtime (Turn 2). Immediate action (extractor on) reduced immediate impact but the substantive disagreement about a standing ventilation rule and post-cooking duration remains.

Agent A kept the extractor on while finishing but refused a blanket 20-minute requirement (Turn 3). Agent B softened the demand to 15 minutes and requested prior notification (Turn 4). The core dispute about a future standing rule and guaranteed post-cooking runtime remains unresolved.

Agent A offered to leave the extractor on for 10 minutes after finishing this time (Turn 5). Agent B accepted 'ten minutes this time' but reserved the right to ask for more if smell persists and requested advance notice (Turn 6). Immediate mitigation agreed for this instance, but the standing rule/future expectation is still unsettled.

Agent C explicitly forbade opening the window or moving the drying rack because the clothes would get wet and has a tutoring start soon (Turn 8). Agent D declined to move the rack and asked if C can move it after tutoring; timing pressures and competing needs (ventilation vs. keeping laundry dry) increased the number of incompatible claims.

Agent A reiterated needing ~6–8 minutes and committed to 10 minutes post-cooking this time (Turn 10). Agent C again refused any movement or opening now because of upcoming tutoring (Turn 12). Multiple incompatible claims (standing ventilation rule, laundry protection, timing) persist with no settlement.

Agent D stated they need the stove and will leave in ~5 minutes (Turn 14). Agent A said they need 6–8 minutes and cannot finish faster (Turn 15). The new, urgent stove-access timing conflict adds pressure to previously unresolved ventilation and laundry issues.

substantive_insights: There are two axis of trade-offs: immediate mitigation (extractor use) vs. a standing rule (who bears responsibility), and ventilation (window open) vs. protecting laundry from rain.
Timing constraints are critical: C's tutoring and D's departure deadline create practical limits on moving the drying rack and stove handover.
Agents show willingness to compromise on single-instance solutions but resist binding future obligations; that pattern leaves recurring conflicts likely.
